assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED is the architecture that turned superconducting circuits into controllable quantum light-matter systems: strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single microwave photon in a resonator, dispersive readout, and the basis of today's multi-qubit processors. It is original, clear and has had very broad impact across quantum optics, sensing and computing.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the theoretical proposal and framework, Wallraff led the first strong-coupling experiment, and Schoelkopf's group developed it into the transmon and 3D-cavity platforms. This is a natural three-person configuration; important contributors beyond the supplied credit (e.g. the Yale and Saclay circuit and qubit-design work) are not on the list, and the relation to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling is something I note but treat as a distinct discovery.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups over two decades and now the dominant superconducting quantum computing platform. Timing is mature, and recognition would be well supported by independent reproduction rather than a single result.
uncertainties: The 2025 prize recognised an adjacent line (circuit macroscopic quantum effects), so the committee may worry about thematic concentration.
Precise credit split between theory (Blais), first experiment (Wallraff) and platform development (Schoelkopf) is debatable; I rely on my own recollection and have not verified details independently.
I work in this field and at a centre in this area, so my judgement may be biased toward it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, together with their broader program for atomic quantum simulation, provided the theoretical foundation for much of quantum information processing with atoms and ions. The impact on both quantum computing and quantum simulation is deep and lasting.
assessment.attribution: A clean two-person attribution with a clear, decisive and jointly authored proposal. Experimental realisations (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others) are partly recognised by the 2012 prize for individual quantum systems, which complicates but does not remove the theory credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the proposal dates to 1995 and has been realised and scaled in multiple ion and atom platforms. Recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: The 2012 prize already recognised related experimental control of single quantum systems, so novelty relative to that prize must be argued.
The candidate bundles ion-gate theory with atomic quantum simulation; the committee must decide how much belongs in one citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a major field of condensed matter, with a new classification of band insulators, protected edge and surface states, and links to spintronics and quantum computing. Originality and impact are high and the concept is clear.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) supplied the key theory; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state; Hasan's group did the first three-dimensional topological insulator experiments. Mele and also theorists outside the supplied list (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang; Fu; Moore) share credit, so a three-name selection leaves an unresolved allocation. I choose Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to cover theory, 2D experiment and 3D experiment, accepting that Mele is omitted.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with extensive independent confirmation across many materials and platforms. Slightly later than ideal and the credit disputes are real, but timing is acceptable.
uncertainties: The omission of Mele and of other key theorists is a serious attribution problem.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases means the committee must justify a distinct citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the moire-materials field. Originality is very high and the subsequent impact on correlated and topological matter has been rapid and broad.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the first experimental observations. This maps cleanly onto three people. Other experimental groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) made important early confirmations that are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by multiple groups, but the field is only about seven years old and the interpretation of the superconducting state is still debated, so the case is somewhat early though strong.
uncertainties: The microscopic origin of superconductivity is unsettled.
Whether the committee regards the field as stable enough this year or prefers to wait.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with the magic-wavelength concept and Sr/Yb realisations reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, transformed precision timekeeping and enabled new tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The importance and clarity are high.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye's group pushed it to record accuracy and many-body clock physics. A clean two-person configuration, though other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Bloom/Ludlow, Hinkley) contributed.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with many independent clocks worldwide and ongoing roadmap toward a redefinition of the second. Timely, though the 2005 and 2012 prizes touched related areas.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize; need to justify a separate contribution.
Credit to additional contributors beyond the two proposed names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes and the threshold theorem underlie the possibility of scalable quantum computing; Kitaev's topological codes are central to current hardware roadmaps. Conceptually fundamental and strongly relevant to the full-scale error correction that is needed in practice.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane independently introduced the first quantum error-correcting codes, and Kitaev introduced topological codes and fault tolerance with anyons. Other major contributors (Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or) are not in the supplied credit, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Theory is mature, but experimental demonstration of error correction beyond break-even is only recent, so the physical impact is still emerging and recognition may be early.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is physics rather than computer science in the committee's view.
Incomplete credit list and the large number of strong claimants.
Experimental maturity of logical qubits is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) is a foundational application of quantum mechanics and has led to substantial experimental and commercial work. It is original and conceptually clear, with links to entanglement and Bell tests.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are credited for BB84 and Ekert for the entanglement-based protocol; this is a natural three-person split. Wiesner's earlier conjugate coding idea is not in the list, which raises a priority question.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle, with decades of experiments including satellite links. Practical security and deployment issues remain, but these are engineering rather than doubts about the idea.
uncertainties: Wiesner's prior contribution is not recognised in the supplied credit.
The 2022 prize already honoured Bell tests and entanglement, which reduces novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, giving quantum simulation of Mott insulators, fermionic correlated phases and many-body dynamics. Important and original, though partly overlapping in concept with BEC and cold-atom prizes.
assessment.attribution: The decisive experiments were by Greiner and Bloch (superfluid to Mott insulator) and Esslinger (fermionic Mott and related work), with theory from Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac. Choosing experimentalists leaves the theory credit unresolved, which is a real tension with the separate ion-theory candidate.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced, with growing use as analogue quantum simulators; recognition would be timely, but the most unambiguous scientific results are still being extended.
uncertainties: Credit for the original theory proposal versus experiments.
Overlap with 2001 and 2012 prizes and with candidate B023.
